content: Mothers who receive conflicting advice or are provided information in a mechanical or impersonal manner often feel undermined in their breastfeeding journey. Many healthcare workers report limited knowledge about breastfeeding and lack confidence in their ability to support mothers effectively. Providing clear guidance to healthcare workers on the minimum support all mothers need, as well as training to address common breastfeeding challenges, can be beneficial. This approach enables healthcare workers to assess infant health and feeding, while offering tailored, sensitive support to breastfeeding mothers that considers their social and cultural context. Such support can help mothers overcome challenges they may face. For more complex breastfeeding issues, collaboration or referral to specialists may be necessary. Focused and optimal immediate support for initiating and establishing breastfeeding within the first hours and days of life has long-term benefits beyond the hospital stay. Evidence shows that immediate and uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact, ideally starting within the first 10 minutes after delivery (and often sooner, within 2–3 minutes), while continuing necessary assessments and care, promotes breastfeeding success. Skin-to-skin contact should last for at least one hour, and longer periods should be encouraged if well-tolerated by both mother and infant. Early initiation of breastfeeding within the first hour after delivery has been shown to have significant positive effects. Among healthy term infants, feeding cues may appear within 15–20 minutes after birth, though they may also emerge later. Mothers who cannot initiate breastfeeding within the first hour, such as those recovering from cesarean sections, anesthesia, or medical instability, should still be supported to breastfeed as soon as they are able. Mothers should be empowered to achieve effective breastfeeding, including proper positioning and attachment of their infants, recognizing and responding to hunger and feeding cues, and expressing breast milk when necessary. Expressing breast milk can also help stimulate effective attachment and sucking, especially during the establishment of breastfeeding or when mother and infant are separated. Mothers of infants in neonatal intensive care units should receive sensitive support to enable skin-to-skin contact, recognize their infants’ behavioral cues, and express breast milk effectively soon after birth. Evidence from systematic reviews highlights the importance of exclusive breastfeeding in the first six months of life, followed by the introduction of complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding up to two years and beyond. Early introduction of additional foods or fluids other than breast milk has been shown to reduce breastfeeding rates up to 20 weeks postpartum. Mothers should be discouraged from giving any food or fluids other than breast milk unless medically indicated. Avoiding pacifiers or dummies during the hospital stay has little to no effect on breastfeeding rates at discharge or at 3–6 months postpartum among term infants. However, among preterm infants, non-nutritive sucking or oral stimulation may shorten hospital stays, though it does not significantly impact breastfeeding outcomes. When additional feeds are medically necessary, or direct breastfeeding is not feasible, avoiding feeding bottles and teats among preterm infants increases the likelihood of exclusive breastfeeding up to six months after discharge. Alternative feeding methods, such as cups, spoons, or other devices, are preferable to bottles and teats. Mothers should be supported to make informed decisions about the use of pacifiers, bottles, and teats during their hospital stay, with awareness of the slight risk of interference with breastfeeding. Healthcare workers often express mixed feelings about advising mothers on pacifier use or bottle feeding. Some view these practices as acceptable or even beneficial in certain situations, such as when a mother is struggling or in neonatal intensive care settings where medical care is prioritized over breastfeeding. However, many healthcare workers lack awareness of the potential effects of pacifiers and bottles on breastfeeding. In summary, mothers should be supported to recognize and respond to their infants’ feeding cues and to establish effective breastfeeding practices. For preterm infants unable to breastfeed directly, non-nutritive sucking and oral stimulation may be beneficial until breastfeeding is established. If expressed breast milk or other feeds are medically indicated, alternative feeding methods such as cups or spoons are preferable to bottles and teats.
